summary: A reply by Tom O'Sullivan to RFC 328. He agrees with dropping the minimum Telnet implementation in favor of one standard protocol. He argues that the Data Types and Hide Your Input signals should stay, since other codes are needed for devices like plotters and numerically controlled machines.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 340 argues for keeping two Telnet features: alternate data types and hidden input. The author explains the devices and access keys that could depend on them.

subtitle: Why Telnet should keep data types and input hiding

tldr.problem: A proposed Telnet change raised questions about whether data types and hidden input were still needed.
tldr.mechanism: Tom O'Sullivan argues that alternate data codes support attached equipment, while hidden input protects keys and passwords from being displayed.
tldr.outcome: The RFC proposes keeping both features and suggests ways to handle return to ASCII and the length of concealed input.

today: RFC 340 is a comment on proposed Telnet changes. It records the author's arguments for keeping alternate data types and hidden input.

sections.title: The Proposed Telnet Changes
sections.content:
Tom O'Sullivan responds to proposed changes to Telnet. He considers it reasonable to use one standard protocol rather than a minimum implementation, but recommends retaining Data Types and Hide Your Input.

The rest of the note gives reasons for retaining these two functions.
sections.plainLanguage: The author supports one standard Telnet protocol. He also argues that two features should remain available to users.

sections.title: Support for Non-ASCII Data
sections.content:
Data Types would let a connection use codes other than ASCII. The author gives examples of equipment that may need arbitrary 8-bit codes: a plotter attached to a teletype, numerically controlled machines and experiments that collect sensor data.

He says each alternate code should provide a way to return to ASCII, though the return code need not be identical for every code.
sections.plainLanguage: Some attached devices use codes that are not ASCII. The author wants Telnet to carry those codes and provide a way to return to ASCII.

sections.title: Hiding Access Keys and Passwords
sections.content: Hide Your Input lets a program prevent typed characters from appearing on the user's screen. O'Sullivan says this is important as network database systems use access keys and passwords. He suggests that a program could specify how many characters to hide, with a default length when no length is supplied.
sections.plainLanguage: A user may need to type a password without showing it on the screen. The author suggests letting a program specify how many characters to hide.
